First, we substitute $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{3}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{3}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{3}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{3}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070214/assets/fac2eaeb6dfdda240d2bad7107f7a7e26ff688e89976437a95b99bc3f2ac288f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{3}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$
